claims.text: Sustained elevated-temperature loading in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers causes progressive plastic deformation primarily through interface-mediated dislocation interactions.
Local compositional short-range order modulates the interface-mediated dislocation interactions.
Reducing the individual layer thickness strengthens or reinforces the effects of FCC/BCC interfaces.
Reducing layer thickness shifts creep from a diffusion-dominated regime to dislocation-driven plastic flow.
Reducing layer thickness increases overall creep resistance.
The starting coatings contain alternating nanoscale FCC and BCC high-entropy-alloy layers.
The starting layers exhibit severe lattice distortion and compositional short-range order.
Local short-range order creates spatially variable energy barriers to dislocation nucleation and motion.
FCC/BCC interfaces act as barriers to dislocation motion under sustained elevated-temperature stress.
FCC/BCC interfaces also act as sources for dislocation nucleation under sustained elevated-temperature stress.
Greater local chemical ordering enhances dislocation pinning and increases the force required for dislocation nucleation.
Thinner layers intensify interface effects by reducing the uninterrupted bulk-like region within each layer.
Approximately 5 nm layers will have lower creep rates than approximately 50 nm layers.
Approximately 5 nm layers will show delayed dislocation activation relative to approximately 50 nm layers.
Dislocation-mediated plasticity will be more pronounced in approximately 50 nm layers than in approximately 5 nm layers.
Interface effects and short-range order are less dominant at lower temperatures or in thicker multilayers.
The proposed behavior requires retention of the nanoscale multilayer architecture and significant short-range order, and may fail if coarsening or thermal disorder removes those features.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says thinner layers shift creep toward dislocation-driven flow, but the predicted outcome says dislocation-mediated plasticity is more pronounced in thicker layers and that thinner layers delay dislocation activation. The direction of the proposed thickness-driven mechanism is therefore inconsistent.
